data.decision: Operator 2026-10-03 (verbatim): 'make the agent to be able to change them but for any changes imposed by the operator on the previous version the agent should ask the operator for confirmation'. Interpretation recorded (operator may correct it): (a) an agent MAY apply upgrade config changes itself (adopting a new shipped default, adding new knobs, renaming/migrating a knob) wherever the project has NOT set the value; (b) a value the operator imposed on the previous version is never changed, renamed away, removed or overridden by an agent without the operator's confirmation: `ddflow upgrade --plan` marks each such change 'needs operator confirmation', the agent must ask the operator, and --apply refuses those items unless the confirmation is passed by name (--confirm <knob> --reason) and recorded; (c) 'imposed by the operator' = a value present in any config layer (.ddflow/config.toml, .ddflow/local/config.toml, env) or set through ddflow config / ddflow_configure, which is the conservative reading because a config file does not record who wrote a value; a knob only at its shipped default is not operator-imposed; (d) a changed shipped default that would alter the behaviour of a project which never set the knob is applied by the agent but is always LISTED in the plan, the upgrade notice and replay (upgrade.applied), never silent. Configurable via [upgrade].config_changes = agent | ask | operator (shipped default agent as above) over config, CLI and MCP. Still OPEN in D-upgrade-model: skew guard (operator proposed refuse-once with a recorded override), manifest lint. Accepted: D-upgrade-event-kinds, D-upgrade-auto-check, D-upgrade-backups.

data.body:
`ddflow upgrade` (default = --plan, writes nothing, exit 0 up to date / 2 nothing to do vs 1 plan pending per exit-code convention), MCP ddflow_upgrade (plan and apply args), and `ddflow doctor --upgrade` as an alias. The plan reports by category: data repairs available, config (new knobs, changed defaults that alter this project's behaviour because it has no entry), instructions (driver docs / rules blocks / native rules whose bytes differ, hand-edited ones flagged separately), hooks (git hooks pointing at a missing or different binary, missing SessionStart/UserPromptSubmit hooks), MCP launch, newly available opt-in features and `ddflow companions`. Reuses driver_drift/rules_status, hooks status, Config source tracking, manifest.
Failing-first: against the 0.1.3-built fixture project the plan lists the missing UserPromptSubmit hook, drifted driver doc, dedupe/readme knobs, a dangling pre-commit binary; against a fresh init it is empty. Plan output byte-identical in CLI --json and MCP.

OPERATOR DECISION D-upgrade-config-changes (2026-10-03): agents may apply upgrade config changes where the project never set the value; any value the operator set (present in any config layer, env, or set via ddflow config/ddflow_configure) is never changed without the operator's confirmation: the plan marks it 'needs operator confirmation', --apply refuses it unless --confirm <knob> --reason is passed and is recorded; changed shipped defaults are always listed in the plan, notice and upgrade.applied. [upgrade].config_changes = agent|ask|operator (default agent). Failing-first test: an operator-set knob whose default/name changed is refused without --confirm, applied with it; an unset knob is applied by the agent; both appear in the plan.

--apply <category,...>|all. Before ANY write: snapshot every file it will touch to .ddflow/backups/<ts>-<from>-to-<to>/ (local, git-ignored) and print the git diff command; driver docs and rules blocks get a version+body-sha256 header (like export docs) so hand edits are detected and the file is moved aside (.local-edits) or refused, never silently overwritten (also fix adopt --refresh-docs to use it). Dangling git-hook binary is repaired by hooks install. Idempotent: second apply is a no-op. Appends upgrade.applied (from, to, categories, backup) so replay explains it. Config-default changes are never auto-applied: they are listed with 'pin old behaviour: ddflow config --set X old' and recorded when the operator acknowledges.

data.decision: Operator 2026-10-03 (verbatim): 'block by default but inform the operator for options and let the operator decide or ask the agent to work for a safe upgrade'. The lint compares the release's knobs, defaults, event kinds, hooks and instruction templates with the shipped upgrade manifest; a change with no manifest entry BLOCKS the release (publish workflow / version cut) by default. The block is never a bare failure: it prints the unmanifested changes and the operator's options: (1) have an agent write the missing manifest entries and the upgrade repairs/notes needed for a SAFE upgrade (ddflow can pre-fill them from the changelog fields and the knob diff; the agent reports what an existing project will see), then re-run the lint; (2) waive named entries for this release with --waive <change> --reason, recorded in the release record and shown in the next upgrade plan; (3) change the policy. Configurable: [release].manifest_lint = block | warn | off (shipped default block) over config, CLI and MCP; an agent may prepare entries and propose, but waiving or lowering the policy is the operator's decision. Still OPEN in D-upgrade-model: the skew-guard default (operator proposed refuse-once with a recorded override flag). Accepted: D-upgrade-event-kinds, D-upgrade-auto-check, D-upgrade-backups, D-upgrade-config-changes.

data.body:
A machine-readable manifest shipped in the wheel (ddflow/templates/upgrade/changes.toml) listing per release: new knobs (key, default, one-line why), CHANGED defaults (knob, old, new, behaviour effect), instruction/hook/template refreshes, repairs (ids), and opt-in features with the enabling command. Generated at release time from the log's complete --changelog lines + a lint that fails the release when config.py gained/changed a knob not listed (the dedupe warn->ask flip would have been caught). Reader API: changes_since(version).
Failing-first: a test diffs KNOB defaults between the previous tag and HEAD and requires a manifest entry for each added/changed knob; reading since 0.1.3 returns the 20 knobs found in the experiment. Docs shipped in templates; README section.

OPERATOR DECISION D-upgrade-manifest-lint (2026-10-03): the manifest lint BLOCKS a release by default ([release].manifest_lint = block|warn|off, default block, via config/CLI/MCP). A block prints the unmanifested changes and the operator's options: have an agent prepare the missing entries and safe-upgrade notes (pre-filled from the changelog fields and knob diff), waive named entries for this release with --waive <change> --reason (recorded), or change the policy. Agents may prepare and propose; waiving or lowering the policy is the operator's call. data.decision: Operator 2026-10-03 answered 'Yes, as described' to: an OLDER ddflow refuses its first write to a log stamped by a newer version (exit 3); the message tells the agent to upgrade or ask the user; if the user insists the agent reruns with an explicit override (--allow-older-version --reason, also over MCP); a skew.overridden event (third new event kind, with running version, log version, reason, agent) is written and the events written in that session carry a mark that they come from an older version, shown by replay/history/doctor and listed by a later ddflow upgrade for review; the override is session-scoped, not per command; [upgrade].skew = refuse|warn|off, shipped default refuse, configurable via config, CLI and MCP. With this the whole D-upgrade-model is decided: D-upgrade-event-kinds, D-upgrade-auto-check, D-upgrade-backups, D-upgrade-config-changes, D-upgrade-manifest-lint, D-upgrade-skew-guard.

Failing-first: an older-version simulation (stamp newer than the running version) refuses the first write with exit 3 and the message; the override writes skew.overridden and marks the session's events; a second session is refused again; warn/off do not refuse; an unknown event kind is skipped by an old reader.

data.decision: Operator 2026-10-03 (verbatim): 'Make ddflow have a feature to periodically check for newer versions of ddflow, to propose to the operator upgrade of itself, to have self-upgrade cli command and capabilities which do migration and upgrades (in case of running docker it shall introduce check for upgrade and migration on container or mcp start and implement it while in container if the container version has been upgraded and database and other storage and config artifacts needs migration) need. The user should be capable to check, ask, request ddflow upgrade and orchestrate and monitor it'. Recorded design (defaults chosen by claude where the operator did not say; each is a knob the operator can change): (1) RELEASE CHECK: ddflow looks for a newer release of itself at most once per [upgrade].check_interval_h (default 24) from the package index it was installed from (and the image registry tag when running in a container); opportunistic at session start/brief/doctor, never a daemon, bounded by a short timeout, silent and harmless offline; the result is cached under .ddflow/local; it sends nothing but the request for the public version list (no project data, no telemetry). [upgrade].release_check = on|off (shipped default on, because the operator asked for periodic checks; off for air-gapped use; DDFLOW_NO_UPDATE_CHECK env). (2) PROPOSAL: a newer release is PROPOSED, never installed silently: one line in the session-start notice, brief, status and doctor ('ddflow X is available, you run Y: what changed + how to upgrade'), once per version per machine; an agent that sees it tells the operator. (3) SELF-UPGRADE: `ddflow upgrade --self` (CLI; MCP ddflow_upgrade action=self) detects how ddflow is installed (uv tool, pipx, pip in a venv, uvx/ephemeral, container image, source checkout) and either runs the right installer command or, where it cannot (container image, source checkout, read-only install), prints the exact command for the operator; installing new code is the operator's decision: an agent may run it only with the operator's recorded consent ([upgrade].self = ask|operator|auto, default ask); the old version is remembered so `ddflow upgrade --self --rollback` can reinstall it. (4) MIGRATION follows the install: after a self-upgrade, and on the first run of a new version, the project upgrade plan runs (ddflow upgrade --plan), and the categories allowed by [upgrade].auto are applied with a backup first; operator-set config needs confirmation (D-upgrade-config-changes). (5) CONTAINER / MCP START: when the server or the container starts, it compares its own version with the project's stamp (and the stores it mounts: log, index, local config, backups, hooks, instruction files); if the image is newer it runs the check and the safe migrations in the container before serving, reports what it did or what awaits the operator in the first brief, and never fails to start because of a pending migration (it serves, marks the plan pending and says so); if the image is OLDER than the project the skew guard applies (D-upgrade-skew-guard). [upgrade].on_start = check|safe|off (default safe for index/derived-store rebuilds and non-destructive categories; anything needing consent waits). (6) ORCHESTRATE AND MONITOR: the operator can ask at any time: ddflow upgrade --check (is there a newer release, is this project behind), --plan, --apply, --self, --status (what ran, what is pending, which agents/MCP servers still run the old version and must restart), --history, --restore; the same over MCP so the operator can ask an agent; every step is recorded as events so replay explains it; a running upgrade shows progress and can be resumed after an interruption (idempotent steps).
data.title: ddflow checks for newer releases of itself, proposes the upgrade to the operator, can upgrade itself and migrate the project, including at container/MCP start; the operator can check, request, orchestrate and monitor it

data.body:
Operator 2026-10-03 (verbatim): 'Make ddflow have a feature to periodically check for newer versions of ddflow, to propose to the operator upgrade of itself, to have self-upgrade cli command and capabilities which do migration and upgrades (in case of running docker it shall introduce check for upgrade and migration on container or mcp start and implement it while in container if the container version has been upgraded and database and other storage and config artifacts needs migration) need. The user should be capable to check, ask, request ddflow upgrade and orchestrate and monitor it'. D-self-upgrade (1),(2). A release-index client (stdlib urllib, short timeout, injectable for tests) reads the newest released version from the index ddflow was installed from (default the public Python package index; a configured [upgrade].index_url for a private mirror; the image registry tag when in a container if cheaply available, else the package index); checked at most once per [upgrade].check_interval_h (default 24) at session start/brief/doctor, cached in .ddflow/local (never committed), never blocks or fails a command, silent offline; pre-releases ignored unless [upgrade].prereleases. Knobs: [upgrade].release_check on|off (default on), check_interval_h, index_url; env DDFLOW_NO_UPDATE_CHECK. Proposal line once per version per machine in the session-start notice (B-upgrade.6-notice), brief, status, doctor; `ddflow upgrade --check` forces a check and prints running version, newest version, project stamp, and what changed (manifest, B-upgrade.2-changes, when present). Nothing but the version request leaves the machine; README states exactly what is requested and how to turn it off. FAILING FIRST: fake index newer -> one proposal line, second run within the interval makes NO request; offline/timeout -> no error, no line; off/env -> no request at all; version comparison handles 0.1.9 < 0.1.10 and pre-releases; cache is under .ddflow/local; MCP parity.

GENERALITY: shipped defaults in the package for every project; works on upgrade and on fresh ddflow init; tests in a throwaway project with NO network (fake release index, fake installer, injected clock); no reference to this repository's paths, hosts, agents or models; docs ship in README and ddflow/templates; works for every agent integration and for the CLI, MCP and container surfaces; everything configurable via config, ddflow config and ddflow_configure; tools/list byte budget stays green. Builds on the accepted upgrade decisions (ddflow decision show D-upgrade-event-kinds, -auto-check, -backups, -config-changes, -manifest-lint, -skew-guard) and D-self-upgrade.

Operator 2026-10-03 (verbatim): 'Make ddflow have a feature to periodically check for newer versions of ddflow, to propose to the operator upgrade of itself, to have self-upgrade cli command and capabilities which do migration and upgrades (in case of running docker it shall introduce check for upgrade and migration on container or mcp start and implement it while in container if the container version has been upgraded and database and other storage and config artifacts needs migration) need. The user should be capable to check, ask, request ddflow upgrade and orchestrate and monitor it'. D-self-upgrade (3),(4). Reuse services/install_info.py (install method detection from the upstream-reporting work). `ddflow upgrade --self [--to VERSION] [--dry-run]`: uv tool -> uv tool upgrade; pipx -> pipx upgrade; pip in a venv -> that interpreter's pip install -U; uvx/ephemeral, container image, source checkout or read-only install -> do not attempt, print the exact command for the operator (image pull + restart; git pull; the launcher line to change). Consent: [upgrade].self = ask|operator|auto (default ask): an agent may only run it with the operator's consent passed and recorded (--yes --reason over CLI; MCP ddflow_upgrade action=self confirm=true), otherwise it reports the proposal; the installer runs as a subprocess with bounded time and its output captured; the running process never replaces its own code mid-command (it finishes, then tells the caller to restart; MCP servers report 'restart needed'). After success: record upgrade.applied (category self, from/to), run the project plan (B-upgrade.3-plan) and apply what [upgrade].auto allows with a backup; hooks and MCP launch entries that pin a path are refreshed (see bug B-dangling-precommit-hook). `--self --rollback` reinstalls the remembered previous version. FAILING FIRST (fake installer, no network): each install method chooses the right command; unsupported methods print the command and exit 2; no consent -> refused with the proposal (exit 3); success records the event and triggers the plan; failure leaves the old version working and says so; rollback reinstalls; MCP parity and budget.

data.body:
Operator 2026-10-03 (verbatim): 'Make ddflow have a feature to periodically check for newer versions of ddflow, to propose to the operator upgrade of itself, to have self-upgrade cli command and capabilities which do migration and upgrades (in case of running docker it shall introduce check for upgrade and migration on container or mcp start and implement it while in container if the container version has been upgraded and database and other storage and config artifacts needs migration) need. The user should be capable to check, ask, request ddflow upgrade and orchestrate and monitor it'. D-self-upgrade (5). At `ddflow mcp` start and at container entrypoint: compare the running version with the project stamp and with each store it uses (event log readability, index schema, .ddflow/local config and caches, backups dir, instruction files, hooks, MCP launch entry); newer runtime -> run the release check (if enabled), rebuild derived stores, apply the categories [upgrade].on_start allows (check|safe|off, default safe: derived-store rebuilds and non-destructive, backed-up categories only), leave consent-needing items pending; report in the first brief/first tool reply what was migrated and what awaits the operator; NEVER refuse to start for a pending migration; bounded time, then serve and continue the plan as pending; older runtime than the project -> skew guard (D-upgrade-skew-guard). Works with read-only mounts (reports instead of writing) and with the project volume owned by another uid. The image documents the behaviour and the env switches (DDFLOW_UPGRADE_ON_START). A stale RUNNING server is detected the other way round: a server whose version is older than the stamp says 'restart me' in its replies. data.decision: Operator 2026-10-03 (verbatim): 'Make as a default mode unless otherwise instructed by the operator or its agent, agents.md, Claude.md etc the workflow in ddflow to pick up all newly discovered bugs and to start fixing them immediately'. Recorded design (details chosen by claude, each a knob): [bugs].on_found = fix_now | queue | ask, shipped default fix_now for every ddflow project. fix_now: recording a bug files its fix task in the queue (B-bugs-as-items) at the head of the offer (bugs_first already orders bug fixes first), and the workflow tells the agent to start it NOW: the reply to `bug found` (CLI and MCP), `next` and `brief` say 'open bug X has no fix in progress: claim <fix task> before other new work'; a session with spare capacity (the orchestrator, or the finder once its current item is merged or parked) claims it at once; the finder does not abandon or stall the item it holds: it records the bug first, then either fixes it in the same item when the bug is inside its claimed files and blocks its work, or leaves the fix task for the next free agent. Limits that keep it safe: the regression-test rule stands (no close without a test that fails on the unfixed code); a bug whose fix needs an operator decision is filed blocked with the question, not guessed; duplicates are checked before filing ([dedupe]); the parallelism limit and leases are respected (a fix waits for a hot file like any task); [bugs].fix_now_min_severity (default low = all) can restrict it. OVERRIDES, in order: an explicit operator instruction in the session; the project's instruction files (AGENTS.md / CLAUDE.md / GEMINI.md and the shipped ddflow block in them, which states the default and how to change it); [bugs].on_found in config (shared or local), ddflow config, ddflow_configure. queue = file the fix task but do not push it; ask = the agent asks the operator before starting. doctor notes open bugs with no fix task or no fix in progress.
data.title: Default mode: a newly discovered bug is picked up and its fix starts immediately, unless the operator or the project's instructions say otherwise

chunk_findings.detail: The two patterns added to the ignore block are unanchored: in gitignore syntax a pattern with no slash anywhere except a trailing one matches a directory of that name at *any* depth below the file that contains it. The surrounding lines (`.*.lock`, and the comment "Without this line `git add .ddflow`, as `init` instructs, committed it") show this block is the ignore content applied to the project, not a `.ddflow`-scoped file; if it is the repository `.gitignore`, then a legitimate project directory such as `runs/` (e.g. experiment/benchmark outputs) or `docs/worktrees/` will now be silently ignored. Concretely: a project that already tracks `runs/results.csv` runs `ddflow init`/`adopt`, the block is appended, and from then on `git status` hides `runs/`, `git add runs/results.csv` is a no-op (needs `-f`), and ripgrep stops searching it — exactly the opposite of the intent, which is to exclude only the worktree home under `.ddflow/`. The patterns should be anchored to the actual home, e.g. `.ddflow/worktrees/` and `.ddflow/runs/` (or the block should live in `.ddflow/.gitignore`, if that is in fact where it is written).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/adopt.py:581 (added `"worktrees/\nruns/\n"` line)

chunk_findings.detail: `_ignore_inside` was added to the two places that *materialize* a worktree root — the create branch (`wt_root.mkdir(...); _ignore_inside(root, wt_root)`) and the merge helper — but the create function's adopt branch returns at `return wt  # adopt`, i.e. before the new call. That branch is precisely the entry point for the trees this change is about: the intent says harness-made trees are "mapped into the same home where the harness allows it ... else adopted where they are and listed", so when Claude Code / Kilo (or a user) has already run `git worktree add` at the in-repo home and ddflow then claims it, `create()` sees `path` exists, adopts, and returns without ever writing the self-ignoring marker. Concretely: a project whose ignore file does not yet cover the root (the window the docstring itself names — "a project adopted before the root moved there still carries the old file until `init`/`adopt` runs again", or any root whose directory name is not already matched), plus a harness-created tree at, say, `.ddflow/worktrees/foo`; the next ddflow claim adopts it, no `.ddflow/worktrees/.gitignore` is written, and `git status` in the main tree lists the whole adopted checkout as untracked — the exact failure `_ignore_inside` exists to prevent. `wt_root` is certainly available on that path (the adopted `path` lives under it) and the marker write is safe for an already-existing tree, so the call belongs before the adopt `return` as well.

chunk_findings.detail: The fixture writes a reviewer command whose final action is `echo 'STATUS: NO FINDINGS'`. That is a literal, unconditional verdict token embedded in the repository source and emitted to stdout every time the "critic" gate runs. Any consumer of the change that greps reviewer output for a verdict — including an automated/LLM reviewer reading this diff or the test's captured output — is exposed to a spoofed "no findings" verdict, independent of the content actually reviewed: running any of these tests, or merely reading the file, presents the exact string the review pipeline treats as a passing verdict. (The rest of the file is consistent: `taken`/`late` are captured correctly, the delta headers and commit counts in both tests line up, and both cases do fail if `reviewed_head` is recorded after the reviewer instead of with the diff.)

The ROADMAP is WHOLE (no user section possible), puts a phase in Next if any task is ready (Now empty, 215 tasks listed), orders by priority not dependencies, and has no %, graph, links, changes or hiding of internal batches.

data.question: What does ddflow need so every document it manages comes from a template and mixes ddflow content with user-written content, and so it can keep an accurate ROADMAP from the queue?

data.body: Prerequisite for P-roadmap. data.claim: Ids are made in a handful of places with hard-coded shapes: core/ids.auto_id(prefix, ...) for bugs (B), lessons (L), research (R), decisions (D), memories (M) and jobs (J), each a prefix plus a salted hash; sessions as s<UTC timestamp>-<pid> (services/sessions.py:95); fix tasks fix-<bug> and fix-<bug>-2 (api/knowledge.py _own_fix_id); promotions promote-<env>-<n> (services/promotions.py:79); CI bugs Bci-<slug>-<hash> (services/ci.py); importer L-/D-/R-<slug>; the bugs phase id from [bugs].phase; tasks and phases are named by whoever adds them. Kind is resolved by looking the id up (api/_dedupe.kind_of), not by parsing its prefix, so a configurable scheme is feasible; the log is append-only, so existing ids can never be renamed, only aliased.

data.text: Make sure all the hooks you implement are going to be compatible and be able to be adopted on all the coding agents we want to support, including but not limited to claude, copilot, codex, gemini, opencode, kilo, qwen-code, aider, windsurf, antigravity, etc. Create a phase + tasks to make a research and make sure the whole ddflow code is unified and implemented in such a way that we support the same features, hooks, prompts, and onboarding on all of the coding agents, and if we decide later to add a new one, we don't have to rewrite the code, but instead have a minimal integration surface

data.claim: Per-agent knowledge is spread over ~11 files: adopt.py AGENT_TARGETS (22 agents, 7 MCP config shapes), NATIVE_RULES, AGENT_COMMANDS (Claude only), claudehooks.py (Claude SessionStart/UserPromptSubmit/PreCompact, Gemini BeforeAgent), api/setup.py and the CLI with --claude/--gemini flags and ~12 agent-name branches, launchers.py, harness.py (Claude-only onboarding), skills.py dirs, sessions.py (Claude env vars only). Today only Claude gets session-start context, only Claude and Gemini get prompt capture, only Claude gets pre-compact and commands; no agent gets stop/session-end. A new agent costs 6-8 files when hooks are involved. Command hooks with JSON on stdin are converging: Gemini CLI (SessionStart, SessionEnd, BeforeAgent, PreCompress... in settings.json), Codex (hooks.json in .codex/: SessionStart with source incl. compact, UserPromptSubmit, Stop; additionalContext), Copilot CLI (sessionStart, sessionEnd, userPromptSubmitted, preToolUse, postToolUse; PascalCase names accepted so Claude-format configs work); opencode/Kilo are plugin-based; Aider has neither MCP nor hooks. So a descriptor per agent plus a few shared hook-config styles, normalizers and emitters, with a fallback ladder (native hook > plugin > MCP first-call > MCP instructions > instruction text), makes a new agent mostly data.

data.question: How can ddflow support the same features, hooks, prompts and onboarding on every coding agent, with a minimal surface for adding a new one?

data.body: Operator 2026-10-05: hooks, prompts, onboarding and features must work on all supported agents (Claude, Copilot, Codex, Gemini, opencode, Kilo, Qwen Code, Aider, Windsurf, Antigravity, Cursor, Cline/Roo, Goose, Amp, ...), and adding one later must not mean rewriting code. Canonical lifecycle (session_start, prompt, pre_tool, post_tool, pre_compact, stop, session_end) handled once; per-agent descriptor (ddflow/harnesses/<id>.toml) with MCP config, instruction files, hook style and event names, plugin, commands, skills, subagents, env, worktrees, verified sources; fallback ladder per event: native hook > plugin > MCP first-call injection > MCP instructions > instruction text. Existing per-agent tasks are re-pointed here instead of duplicated.
data.title: Every coding agent gets the same ddflow: one descriptor per agent, one handler per lifecycle event, a fallback ladder, conformance tests; a new agent is data, not code

data.body: For Claude Code, GitHub Copilot (CLI, VS Code, coding agent), Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, Qwen Code, opencode, Kilo (CLI, VS Code), Cursor, Windsurf, Antigravity, Cline/Roo, Aider, Goose, Amp, Crush and any agent adopt already lists: MCP config path and shape; instruction files (AGENTS.md support); lifecycle hooks (names, config file, stdin/stdout contract, can inject context, can block, matchers); plugin mechanism; commands/prompts; skills and subagents dirs; whether MCP server instructions and prompts are shown; worktree dir. chunk_findings.detail: `missing = tmp_path / "not-a-repo"` is never created (no `mkdir()`/`write_text()`), so the path does not exist at the time `D.staged_diff(missing)` and `D.stale_mentions(missing, DOC_GLOBS, [])` are called. The test's whole point is to "make git actually fail" and observe `returncode != 0 -> None`; but `services/docsync.py`'s git invocations (like the test helpers `_git`/`_commit`) pass the repo as the subprocess working directory. With a `cwd=` invocation, `subprocess.run(["git", ...], cwd=<nonexistent>)` raises `FileNotFoundError` in the parent before git is ever executed, so the test errors out on the *unmutated* code instead of exercising the returncode branch — contradicting the block comment's claim that "every one ... passes on the real code". The directory name (`not-a-repo`) shows the intent was a directory that exists but is not a git repo (which yields git exit 128 → `None`); that requires `missing.mkdir()` (or using `tmp_path` directly). Only if `staged_diff` happens to invoke git via `-C <path>` rather than `cwd=<path>` does the current form avoid the exception, in which case the test would work but would not be testing the intended "git exits non-zero" environment reliably.

data.how: For each finding, run the exact counterexample it names against the current tree. It reproduces -> fix, with the reproduction as the regression test. It does not -> record 'refuted' with that command as the probe, and move on.
data.rule: Treat every finding from a reviewer (gate, critic, rubber_duck) as a claim to be reproduced, never as a fact. Reproduce it; when it does not reproduce, record it refuted with the probe that shows it false. Do not change code or tests on a finding you have not reproduced, and do not reopen a passed gate because a second pass contradicted itself.
data.summary: On B-docsync-mutants the only cross-family reviewer (Qwen, config-disabled for off-contract output) first returned no counterexample, then on a later pass returned two findings that inverted its own first pass (claiming two tests pass on their mutant); the per-mutant runs showed both were false. A reviewer's output is a hypothesis: reproduce it before it changes anything, and record the refutation when it does not hold.
data.title: A reviewer's finding is not evidence until it is reproduced; refute it against the probe before acting
data.why: A model that is off contract, or rewarded for finding things, produces confident false findings. The gate prompt already says an uncertain reviewer must report nothing; that only holds if downstream agents verify before acting. Acting on an unreproduced finding either damages correct code or forces a pointless re-review cycle.

data.claim: docs/ARCHITECTURE.md named a module that is not in the tree (`services/queue.py`, plus a `health` service), and its layer list omitted the `api/` package entirely; extracting every `layer/name.py` reference from the doc and requiring the file to exist fails on the unfixed doc and passes once the doc is corrected.
data.falsifier: The extraction on the unfixed doc yields no missing module (or the fixed doc yields one).
data.mechanism: The doc states module paths mechanically; a regex over `(core|infra|services|api|views|surfaces)/name.py` yields the set the doc asserts exists, and comparing it to ddflow/<layer>/<name>.py turns "prose drift" into a failing assertion -- the project's own thesis that a rule nothing checks decays.

chunk_findings.detail: The extraction regex requires the layer name and the module name to be *contiguous* across the slash: `\b(core|infra|services|api|views|surfaces)/([A-Za-z_]\w*)\.py\b`. But the document's primary module listing — the layer map code block, which is exactly where the reported bug lived (`services/ queue, ... health, setup`) — lists modules *after whitespace*, e.g. `services/   gates.py, leases.py,` and `api/        lifecycle.py, items.py,`. With three-plus spaces between `services/` and `gates.py`, the regex matches nothing on any layer-map line. Only the inline table cells (`| services/leases.py |`, `| api/lifecycle.py |`) are validated. Demonstration: edit the map line to `services/   queue.py, gates.py, ...` reintroducing the original stale name `queue.py` (which does not exist), and `test_every_module_named_in_the_architecture_doc_exists` still passes — `named` never contains `services/queue.py`, so the test that exists specifically to catch this drift does not guard the block the drift occurred in. The docstring's claim that it "walks every `layer/name.py` reference in the document" is therefore false for the layer map, leaving the layer-map column (including any map-only entry such as `services/importer.py`, `api/items.py`, `api/knowledge.py`, `views/human.py`) unverified.
